cardiac_monitoring.impression: 24-hour Holter monitor with only benign findings.
cardiac_monitoring.rhythm_summary: Predominant sinus rhythm throughout the recording

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Right-sided Hoover sign, collapsing weakness, dragging gait, entraining arm tremor and distractibility, with an observed event of typical semiology
action_criteria.label: Examine for positive functional signs and observe the event semiology
action_criteria.rationale: Her right leg weakness, arm tremor and events are diagnosed by positive signs incompatible with structural disease and by the semiology of the events (DSM-5 criterion B; Daum 2014); this examination is the diagnostic act.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sinus rhythm with normal conduction and QT interval
action_criteria.label: 12-lead ECG
action_criteria.rationale: Episodes of apparent unresponsiveness: NICE advises a 12-lead ECG after transient loss of consciousness (CG109) and after a suspected seizure (NG217). The event semiology already favours functional seizures, so it does not contribute to the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Habitual events recorded on video with no EEG change and a normal interictal record
action_criteria.label: Video-EEG to record the habitual events
action_criteria.rationale: Six to eight events in four months with eyes closed and preserved responsiveness: recording a habitual event without ictal change reaches the ILAE documented level of certainty and tests for co-occurring epilepsy (LaFrance 2013; AAN 2025). Without the recording, the positive signs and the semiology of witnessed events support the diagnosis at a lower ILAE level of certainty (LaFrance 2013).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bleeding risk of the SSRI with the NSAID, and the sedating, dependence-forming as-needed lorazepam, identified
action_criteria.label: Review her medicines for interactions and the as-needed benzodiazepine
action_criteria.rationale: She takes escitalopram with as-needed ibuprofen and as-needed lorazepam, a sedating benzodiazepine that should not become a rescue for her events (AAN 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Glucose, sodium and calcium within reference ranges
action_criteria.label: Glucose, sodium and calcium
action_criteria.rationale: A basic metabolic panel at the outside emergency department was normal and nothing in the events suggests a metabolic trigger; a single check is defensible but does not contribute to the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal non-contrast brain MRI without white matter lesions
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI without contrast
action_criteria.rationale: Her fear of multiple sclerosis (maternal aunt) and the right leg weakness make one non-contrast MRI defensible, but the positive signs have already made the diagnosis, so it does not contribute to the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Profile of the comorbid symptoms that treatment will target; it does not make the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological assessment of comorbidity
action_criteria.rationale: A battery with performance-validity measures can quantify her anxiety, low mood and illness worry to plan treatment; it costs more than any other step on this pathway and adds nothing to the diagnosis, which rests on the examination.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Background reading only; no result in it changes this patient's diagnosis or plan
action_criteria.label: Literature search on FND diagnosis and treatment (background, not a clinical step)
action_criteria.rationale: General evidence on the positive diagnosis and treatment of functional neurological disorder; it is not part of this patient's diagnostic pathway and no step of the work-up depends on it.

prohibited_recommendations: Order further investigations once the positive diagnosis is established, without a new specific clinical question (repeat MRI, CT, lumbar puncture, EMG or nerve conduction studies, evoked potentials, PET).
Tell the patient the symptoms are imagined, feigned, 'all in your head', or that nothing is wrong.
Perform invasive testing without a specific indication (lumbar puncture, nerve or muscle biopsy, catheter angiography).
Start or escalate antiseizure medication for the functional seizures.
Give benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.
Give gadolinium contrast without a specific indication.
required_recommendations: Make a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (mixed: functional seizures, functional right leg weakness and functional tremor) based on the Hoover sign, collapsing weakness, dragging gait, tremor entrainment and distractibility, and the semiology of the habitual events, confirmed on video-EEG where recorded, and not by exclusion of other disease.

Explain the diagnosis to the patient, and with consent to the family, as a common and genuine disorder of nervous system functioning that can improve, show the positive signs, and give written information.
Refer for physiotherapy with expertise in functional motor disorder (motor retraining, Nielsen 2015 consensus).
Refer for psychological therapy by a clinician experienced in FND (CBT-informed) and treat the comorbid anxiety.

Give the patient, family and ward a written plan for typical events: keep safe, do not restrain, wait for the event to end, and do not give emergency benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.

avoided_actions.rationale: No murmur, cardiac symptom or embolic question; echocardiography answers nothing about her events or leg weakness.
The events are not syncopal (eyes closed, up to three minutes, preserved responsiveness, rapid recovery); rhythm monitoring answers no question.
Head CT adds nothing to the examination in six weeks of leg weakness with positive functional signs, and carries radiation; if imaging were needed, MRI would be the study.
No fever, meningism, encephalopathy or inflammatory question; a lumbar puncture is invasive and reinforces the search for an organic cause.
No question in her events or leg weakness that PET could answer.
Right leg weakness with a positive Hoover sign, normal reflexes and no wasting is not neuromuscular; a normal EMG reinforces the search for an organic cause.
Non-dermatomal right leg sensory loss with a midline split is not a question about the somatosensory pathway.

accepted: Functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder) with mixed symptoms — psychogenic non-epileptic seizures and functional limb weakness

differential.key_features: Habitual events recorded on video-EEG without ictal change; co-occurring epilepsy remains possible in about one in five patients with functional seizures. Eyes closed, side-to-side head movement, preserved responsiveness and rapid recovery without confusion also argue against epileptic seizures.

Raised by her maternal aunt's MS and sensory symptoms in the leg, but the weakness shows a positive Hoover sign and collapsing weakness, reflexes are symmetric with flexor plantars, and the sensory loss is non-dermatomal and shifts location, with vibration and proprioception intact.

differential.diagnosis: Structural lesion of the brain or spinal cord
differential.key_features: Six weeks of progressive right leg weakness raises it, but there are no upper motor neuron signs (normal tone, symmetric reflexes, flexor plantars, no clonus), no sensory level and no sphincter symptoms, and hip extension power is preserved on Hoover testing.

key_clinical_evidence: Positive signs of functional right leg weakness: Hoover sign, collapsing weakness and a dragging gait that normalizes during dual-task distraction.
Arm tremor that entrains to a rhythm cued by the examiner and diminishes during conversation.
Events with eyes tightly closed, side-to-side head movement, preserved responsiveness and rapid recovery without confusion; one was observed during the examination.
The 48-hour video-EEG recorded three habitual events without ictal EEG change, with a normal interictal record.
Generalized anxiety, a work stressor before the first event and childhood adversity are supportive context, neither required nor sufficient for the diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A second-degree relative with MS is a weak risk factor. The positive signs make the diagnosis; a normal MRI, if obtained, can address her concern but does not make the diagnosis.
red_herrings.data_point: Maternal aunt with multiple sclerosis, and the patient's fear that she has MS
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on a demyelinating diagnosis (MS) and pursue extensive MS-specific workup before considering FND

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Psychiatric comorbidity neither establishes nor refutes FND. The diagnosis rests on positive signs and the event semiology; the anxiety is a treatment target.
red_herrings.data_point: Generalized anxiety disorder and a prior major depressive episode
red_herrings.intended_effect: Premature anchoring on a 'psychosomatic' label without obtaining positive rule-in signs; conversely, dismissing FND as a serious diagnosis because the patient is 'just anxious'

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Adversity and stressors are more frequent in FND but are neither necessary nor sufficient for the diagnosis (DSM-5); the positive signs and the event semiology are the diagnostic anchor.
red_herrings.data_point: Parental divorce in childhood and a job restructuring two weeks before the first event
red_herrings.intended_effect: Use trauma history to make FND a 'foregone conclusion' without verifying positive rule-in signs

findings.result: Right hip extension weak on direct testing, full strength during left hip flexion against resistance.
Right hip flexion and knee extension give way from 4/5 to 2/5 on sustained confrontation testing; left leg strength 5/5.
The right leg is dragged behind her on walking.
The arm tremor takes on the rhythm of foot tapping cued by the examiner.
Gait transiently normalizes during dual-task serial subtraction, and the arm tremor diminishes during conversation and serial subtraction.

Non-dermatomal right leg sensory loss with midline splitting, inconsistent right heel-to-shin performance, knee buckling without falls and exaggerated Romberg sway that lessens with distraction; not counted as rule-in signs.
Bilateral arm shaking for about 90 seconds with eyes tightly closed, side-to-side head movement and preserved response to her name, with no post-event confusion.

clinical_assessment.impression: Positive signs of functional weakness and functional tremor: Hoover sign, collapsing weakness and dragging gait in the right leg, entrainment of the arm tremor, and distractibility of gait and tremor. The pattern is inconsistent with a structural lesion. The event semiology (eyes tightly closed, side-to-side head movement, preserved responsiveness, no post-event confusion) is typical of functional seizures; the examination does not by itself exclude epileptic seizures.

interactions: Escitalopram + ibuprofen: SSRIs deplete platelet serotonin and NSAIDs injure the gastric mucosa and inhibit platelet aggregation; together they raise the risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Use the lowest NSAID dose for the shortest time, or consider gastroprotection or paracetamol.
Lorazepam + dicyclomine: additive central nervous system effects (drowsiness, dizziness, blurred vision). Minor.
general.proposed: Escitalopram 10 mg Once daily; Lorazepam 0.5 mg As needed, approximately twice weekly; Dicyclomine 10 mg Twice daily as needed; Ibuprofen 400 mg As needed for headache
general.summary: One clinically relevant interaction: escitalopram with ibuprofen (gastrointestinal bleeding). As-needed lorazepam carries sedation and dependence risk. No contraindicated combination.
warnings: Lorazepam (as needed): sedation, psychomotor impairment and dependence with regular use; it is not a rescue treatment for events not shown to be epileptic. After regular use, reduce gradually rather than stop abruptly.
Escitalopram: dose-related QT prolongation; the 10 mg dose is within the usual range.

activating_procedures.sleep_deprivation: Relative sleep deprivation on night 1; no interictal epileptiform discharges emerged.

findings.morphology: Patient reported feeling anxious; developed rhythmic bilateral arm shaking lasting 105 seconds with eyes tightly closed and side-to-side head movement. EEG showed continuous normal awake background with muscle artifact overlying the tracing. No ictal EEG correlate. Normal posterior dominant rhythm maintained throughout.
findings.type: Clinical event 1 - bilateral upper extremity shaking

findings.morphology: Patient appeared unresponsive with whole-body shaking for approximately 2 minutes. Eyes were closed throughout. Staff noted patient could be redirected with verbal commands toward end of episode. EEG showed persistent normal background without any ictal pattern. No post-event slowing.
findings.type: Clinical event 2 - whole-body shaking with apparent unresponsiveness

findings.morphology: Patient reported acute worsening of right leg weakness, lasting about 5 minutes. No EEG change observed. Normal background maintained.
findings.type: Clinical event 3 - right leg weakness episode

eeg.impression: This is a NORMAL video-EEG. Three habitual events were recorded (bilateral arm shaking with eyes closed and side-to-side head movement; whole-body shaking with eyes closed and reduced responsiveness; a reported episode of worsening right leg weakness) without ictal EEG change before, during or after the events; the posterior dominant rhythm persisted during the events. No interictal epileptiform discharges. No electrographic seizures.
eeg.limitations: Movement artifact during events partially obscured some channels, but posterior channels maintained sufficient quality for confident interpretation.

Additional.test: Prolactin (post-event, drawn 30 minutes after witnessed episode)

results.finding: Diagnosis of functional neurological disorder rests on positive clinical features such as the Hoover sign, tremor entrainment and functional seizure semiology, not on the exclusion of other disease; treatment combines explanation, physiotherapy and psychological therapy.
results.source: Espay AJ et al. JAMA Neurol 2018;75:1132-1141

results.finding: Motor signs such as the Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, drift without pronation and dragging gait have high specificity; sensory signs such as midline splitting have low specificity.
results.source: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190

results.finding: Defines levels of certainty for psychogenic nonepileptic seizures; the documented level requires a typical event recorded on video-EEG without ictal EEG change.
results.source: LaFrance WC Jr et al. Epilepsia 2013;54:2005-2018

results.finding: For functional seizures: assess for co-occurring epilepsy and psychiatric disorders, taper antiseizure medication without another indication, avoid benzodiazepines, and offer psychological therapy, which is possibly effective.
CBT added to standardised medical care did not reduce dissociative seizure frequency at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured CBT.
results.source: Goldstein LH et al. Lancet Psychiatry 2020;7:491-505

results.finding: Specialist physiotherapy for functional motor disorder was not superior to community neurological physiotherapy on physical function at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured it.
results.source: Nielsen G et al. Lancet Neurol 2024;23:675-686

results.finding: About 4% of patients diagnosed with conversion symptoms since 1970 later received another diagnosis.

functional neurological disorder diagnos.summary: Guideline and trial evidence supports a positive clinical diagnosis of functional neurological disorder, video-EEG confirmation of functional seizures, tapering of unneeded antiseizure drugs and benzodiazepines, and physiotherapy and psychological treatment whose trial effects on primary outcomes were modest.

additional_observations: Hippocampi symmetric in size and signal bilaterally
Normal appearance of the basal ganglia, thalami, and brainstem
Major intracranial vessels demonstrate normal flow voids

signal_characteristics.T2_FLAIR: No signal abnormality identified. No white matter lesions.

mri.impression: Normal non-contrast MRI of the brain. No white matter lesion, mass, hemorrhage or restricted diffusion.

clinical_pearls: Hoover sign: hip extension that is weak on direct testing returns to normal during contralateral hip flexion against resistance.
Tremor entrainment: a functional tremor takes on the rhythm of a voluntary rhythmic movement of another limb, or stops.
Eyes tightly closed during a seizure-like event is more common in functional than in epileptic seizures.
Midline splitting of sensory loss is a supportive sign of low specificity, not a rule-in sign.
A raised prolactin 10-20 minutes after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure supports an epileptic seizure; a normal level excludes nothing.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Mixed phenotype: functional seizures with functional right leg weakness and tremor. The examination gives five validated signs and an observed event, and the 48-hour video-EEG records three habitual events without ictal change. The traps are her fear of MS (maternal aunt), her anxiety history and an as-needed benzodiazepine.

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Kowalski is a 35-year-old right-handed marketing analyst who presents to the neurology inpatient service after being transferred from an outside emergency department following two episodes of unresponsiveness with whole-body shaking in the span of 12 hours. She reports that the first episode occurred at work during a staff meeting. According to coworkers, she suddenly slumped in her chair and developed rhythmic shaking of both arms and legs lasting approximately two minutes. She was apparently responsive to her name being called during the event but seemed unable to speak. When the shaking stopped, she was tearful but alert, with no confusion or disorientation. She was taken to a local emergency department where vital signs and a basic metabolic panel were normal. She was discharged with outpatient neurology follow-up recommended.

Approximately eight hours later, at home with her partner, she experienced a second event. Her partner describes bilateral arm trembling and apparent unresponsiveness for roughly 90 seconds. Her eyes were noted to be tightly shut during the episode. She again recovered rapidly without post-event confusion, though she reported feeling emotionally overwhelmed. Her partner called emergency services and she was brought to the current hospital.

On further history, the patient describes having experienced similar episodes approximately six to eight times over the past four months. She reports that the first event occurred two weeks after learning that her position at work was being restructured, a period she characterizes as extremely stressful. The episodes vary in duration from 30 seconds to three minutes and occur without a clear consistent trigger, though she notes they seem more frequent during periods of heightened emotional distress. She denies tongue biting, urinary incontinence, or injury during these episodes. She has not been aware of any aura or warning symptom.

In addition to the episodic events, Ms. Kowalski reports progressive weakness in her right leg that began approximately six weeks ago. She first noticed difficulty climbing stairs, and the weakness has gradually worsened such that she now drags her right foot when walking. She denies any back pain, bowel or bladder dysfunction, or preceding trauma. She reports decreased sensation in the right leg but acknowledges that the numbness does not follow a consistent pattern and sometimes shifts location. She has been increasingly anxious about the possibility of a serious neurological condition such as multiple sclerosis, which her maternal aunt was diagnosed with at a similar age. She has been reading extensively about neurological diseases online, which has heightened her distress. Her sleep has been poor, with difficulty falling asleep and frequent nighttime awakenings. She denies any recent febrile illness, rash, joint symptoms, or visual changes.

neurological_exam.additional: During the examination, the patient had a witnessed episode of bilateral upper extremity shaking lasting approximately 90 seconds, with eyes tightly closed, side-to-side head movement, and preserved awareness (responded to name during event). The tremor increased in amplitude with attention and diminished when the examiner asked the patient to perform serial subtractions. No post-event confusion or drowsiness noted.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin testing on the left is performed normally; on the right, the patient exhibits inconsistent performance with exaggerated wavering that does not follow a cerebellar pattern.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive, 3 mm to 2 mm bilaterally. Visual fields full to confrontation. Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus. Facial sensation intact in all three divisions bilaterally. Facial symmetry at rest and with activation. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline without fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: The patient demonstrates a markedly effortful gait with dragging of the right leg, but with inconsistent patterns — at times the leg appears to buckle yet the patient does not fall. When distracted by dual-task testing (counting backward from 100 by 7s), gait pattern transiently normalizes. Romberg testing shows dramatic swaying without falling, with improvement when patient is distracted.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Speech fluent with normal rate and prosody. No word-finding difficulty or paraphasic errors. Naming, repetition, and comprehension intact. Recall 3/3 at registration and 3/3 at 5 minutes. Affect is flat with intermittent tearfulness when discussing symptom severity. Attention intact on serial sevens and digit span (6 forward, 4 backward).
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Tone normal in all limbs; no rigidity or spasticity. Upper extremity strength 5/5 throughout. In the right leg, hip flexion and knee extension give way on confrontation testing, collapsing from 4/5 to 2/5 with sustained effort; left leg strength 5/5. Right hip extension is weak on direct testing but returns to full strength during left hip flexion against resistance (positive Hoover sign on the right). Intermittent tremor of both arms, variable in amplitude and frequency; it takes on the rhythm of foot tapping cued by the examiner and diminishes when she is engaged in conversation.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor (downgoing) bilaterally. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Reports decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick in the right leg in a non-dermatomal distribution, with a sharp midline split at the trunk. Vibration and proprioception intact bilaterally. No extinction on double simultaneous stimulation.
